findings.title: Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and resources
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, an unhealthy process is `process.kill()`-ed and a replacement is immediately started via `_create_process_for_shards`, but the old process object is never `join()`-ed. In production (spawn mode) each killed process becomes a zombie until the parent exits, and its `SpansBuffer` (with its Redis connection pool) is dropped from `self.buffers[process_index]` without being closed, leaking connections. Since restarts can happen repeatedly (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process index), a consumer running for a long time can accumulate zombies and leaked Redis connections. The old process should be joined/cleaned up before or after starting the replacement.

findings.title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(shard)` is defined but never called anywhere; the restart path uses `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. Dead code invites confusion about which restart entrypoint to use and should be removed.

findings.title: Per-process restart counters never reset, so cumulative restarts eventually crash the consumer
findings.body: `self.process_restarts[process_index]` is only ever incremented and never reset, even after a process has been running healthily for a long time. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10`, a process that legitimately crashed 11 times over months of uptime (e.g. transient Redis outages) will cause `_ensure_processes_alive` to raise RuntimeError and take down the whole consumer. The counter should be reset once the replacement process has been observed healthy for some period. This was a pre-existing flaw for the single process, but multiplying the number of processes multiplies the probability of hitting it.

findings.title: Tests only cover the threading (produce_to_pipe) path, never the multiprocessing path
findings.body: Both consumer tests and test_flusher.py inject `produce_to_pipe`, which makes `SpanFlusher` use `threading.Thread` and `partial` instead of the spawn-based `multiprocessing.Process` with `run_with_initialized_sentry`. None of the new multi-process behavior (process-per-shard spawn, argument pickling of per-shard SpansBuffer and shared Values, process restart in `_ensure_processes_alive`, join/terminate of real processes) is exercised. The new `test_flusher_processes_limit` test only asserts on dicts/counts, not that processes actually work. A regression in the spawn path (e.g. a pickling error in the new per-shard buffer or the new `shards` argument) would not be caught.

findings.title: test_basic relies on a fixed 0.1s sleep for the flusher thread to observe the drift change
findings.body: `test_basic` sets `current_drift` and then sleeps for 0.1s before `step.join()`, expecting the background flusher thread to have picked up the new drift and flushed the segment. There is no synchronization guaranteeing the thread reached the read of `current_drift` or completed the flush/produce within 100ms, so the `(msg,) = messages` unpacking can flake on slow/loaded CI. A poll-until-assertion loop (with timeout) would make this deterministic.

findings.title: max_processes default of None means one process per shard, contradicting documented default of 1
findings.body: `SpanFlusher.__init__` treats `max_processes=None` as `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, i.e. one process per shard. The `--flusher-processes` CLI option documents "Defaults to 1", and its click default is 1, so CLI-driven deployments get 1; but any other instantiation path that omits the argument (as all existing direct callers in tests and code do) silently spawns one process per assigned partition, each of which re-imports sentry/Django under spawn. This is a significant behavioral/memory difference depending on call path, and the docstring does not mention it. The default should be consistent (e.g. 1) or the behavior documented.
